Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, Robert C. O'Brien's novel that won the Newbery Medal in nineteen seventy-two. Mrs. Frisby is a timid field mouse facing the seasonal destruction of her home by a farmer's plow. She must find a way to move her chronically ill son Timothy to a safe place before spring plowing begins. In her search for help, she encounters a colony of highly intelligent rats who were subjects of a sinister government laboratory experiment at the National Institute of Mental Health. These rats were genetically enhanced through experimental procedures, granting them human-level intelligence, the ability to read, and the capacity to build civilization. They have escaped their laboratory captivity and established an underground society with strict codes of honor, planning to make themselves self-sufficient by stealing grain rather than relying on NIMH's experiments forever. Mrs. Frisby discovers that Justin, the noble rat leader, knew her late husband, Jonathan Frisby, who died in an experiment while helping the rats escape. The rats' leader, Nicodemus, is wise and tormented by the ethics of their enhanced intelligence. They are aware that their powers were granted artificially and debate whether they have the right to use stolen resources. The climax involves Mrs. Frisby's bravery in retrieving a crucial item to help the rats relocate their entire colony. The novel demonstrated that children's literature could tackle scientific ethics and the philosophical depth of artificial enhancement.
